records.name: Mauritius
records.summary:
Mauritius is workable for trans visitors — the Indian Ocean's most liveable jurisdiction. The Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct; the Equal Opportunities Act covers discrimination; and in 2024 Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan competed as the first trans woman in Miss Universe Mauritius — a public milestone met with national discussion rather than violence. There is no legal gender recognition law (a barrier highlighted by AfricLaw), and social conservatism persists, but tourist infrastructure is extensive and accustomed to diverse visitors, and there is no documented police targeting pattern.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning courts, low street risk in tourist areas.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview, last updated 12 March 2026: the Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct — advances noted for lesbian, gay and bisexual people with 'less evident' progress for trans or intersex people. No same-sex marriage or civil unions recognised; Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against sexual-orientation discrimination; intersex newborns may be registered 'undetermined' under the 2021 Civil Status Act but nonconsensual intersex procedures are not banned; legal gender recognition not possible and LGBTI organisations cannot register. Pride held since 2005 with counter-protesters; during the 2024 national elections a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and others used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech.

AfricLaw (23 August 2024, Lakshita Kanhiya): analyses the historic participation of Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan — the first transgender woman in Miss Universe Mauritius 2024 — against the country's legal obstacles: the Civil Status Act of 1981 and Central Population Database as the framework denying recognition, plus pervasive stigmatisation, with activism by the Young Queer Alliance and Association VISA-G. Concludes legal recognition and protection for trans Mauritians remain inadequate despite the visibility milestone.

US State Department 2016 Country Report — Mauritius: Section 250 sodomy statute almost never reached same-sex couples in court (sodomy references overwhelmingly arose in heterosexual divorce cases as an aggravating factor); documents societal discrimination, with LGBTI victims of family verbal abuse or violence reporting to local NGOs including Collectif Arc-en-Ciel and Young Queer Alliance, and harassment of a transgender person for wearing women's clothing. Dated pre-2023 baseline for the record.

Young Queer Alliance policy brief (July 2021): 'Administrative recognition of Trans People in Mauritius' - argues for legal gender recognition; notes the WHO's ICD-11 removed trans categories from mental disorders (2019) and calls on Mauritius to join countries recognising gender identity in law.

records.name: Senegal
records.summary:
Senegal is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises “unnatural acts” (up to 5 years, applied to both men and women), enforcement is active (periodic arrest waves), and anti-LGBT forces are pushing to raise sentences to 15 years. Mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented, and even public discussion is policed: two men were jailed in 2024 for “false news” after accusing the Prime Minister of tolerating homosexuality. There is no legal gender recognition and no visible community infrastructure — Dakar's scene is deeply underground.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest and mob violence.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile: Senegal criminalises same-sex sexual activity (Article 319 of the 1965 Penal Code, up to 5 years' imprisonment). (Only the opening of the profile was retrievable at fetch time.)

76crimes (16 Jul 2024): anti-LGBT forces in Senegal are pushing for 15-year prison sentences for gay sex, up from the current maximum of five years — a debate running since 2020, with abuses against LGBT+ people commonplace in the West African nation.

BBC News: two men were jailed in Senegal for criticising opposition leader Ousmane Sonko — months and fined 100,000 CFA francs ($165, £130) each. They had been angered that Mr Sonko had allowed a visiting French politician to express his support for same-sex marriages. Homosexual acts are banned in the mainly Muslim West African country and are punishable by up to five years in prison. The political activist and the preacher were arrested two weeks ago after posting a video attacking Mr Sonko for giving a platform t

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Senegal: documents preelectoral violence, torture, and 'violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons' among major human-rights problems.

76crimes (24 Sep 2018): four LGBT people — two women and two men — were detained in Dakar for 'acts against the order of nature' amid a wave of politically motivated arrests ahead of the 2019 elections, triggered after videos circulated.

Metro (Nov 2023): a man's body was dug up and burned in the street in Senegal after it was revealed he was gay — exhumed and set on fire in the street after locals are said to have found out he was gay, in a case that has shocked the West African country. Four men have been arrested in connection with the incident, though images from the scene show a crowd of hundreds gathering around the fire. The 31-year-old man, named locally as Cheikh Fall, had been buried in Léona Niassene cemetery i

records.name: Côte d'Ivoire
records.summary:
Côte d'Ivoire is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised, but in late 2024 the country saw a wave of violence: social-media influencers exhorted followers to 'hunt' gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in the largest city (Abidjan).

sources.summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying NYT article (Oct 2024) covers the situation of LGBTQ people in Ivory Coast (Côte d'Ivoire).

UNDP report (Dec 2024) 'African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa' - includes a Côte d'Ivoire country overview assessing the protective legal environment, investigation/prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space, and inclusion of LGBT+ people.

US State Department 2023 report, Côte d'Ivoire: same-sex conduct not criminalised, but LGBTQI+ persons faced violence — three community deaths reported in the year; police responses to non-state violence were sometimes slow and ineffective and often blamed the victim; a transgender man was beaten in Abobo, Abidjan, while walking with another man. Authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Côte d'Ivoire: post-electoral-crisis context (3,000 deaths, sexual violence, displacement) - general human-rights baseline with limited LGBT-specific content.

Critical African Studies (2015), Thomann & Corey-Boulet, 'Violence, Exclusion and Resilience among Ivoirian Travestis': travestis (born anatomically male, living as women) face harsher stigmatization and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity avoids attention, and have been underserved by Ivoirian rights groups that distanced themselves from them; examines isolation after the 2010-11 post-election violence.

Same article via PMC canonical URL (Thomann & Corey-Boulet 2015): the key academic source on trans-feminine people's experiences in Côte d'Ivoire — documented violence and social exclusion of travestis alongside their resilience; duplicate of the ncbi copy retained as canonical mirror.

records.name: Mali
records.summary:
Mali is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. In October-November 2024 the Transitional National Council adopted a new penal code criminalising homosexuality for the first time — with the Justice Minister declaring that anyone “engaging in, promoting or apologising for” same-sex relations will be prosecuted; vague drafting suggests broad application, and prior “public indecency” provisions (Art 225) were already used against gender-nonconforming people. The junta context means no independent judiciary, no civil society space, and active conflict in much of the country.

For a visitor: a brand-new criminalisation statute under a junta with no recourse, plus conflict conditions.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (6 November 2024): Mali’s new penal code criminalises same-sex conduct with harsh penalties; previously legal but vague "public indecency" provisions (Article 225) were used against LGBT people and gender-nonconforming expressions, and the new law bans the undefined "promotion" of homosexuality, greatly expanding who can be prosecuted.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Mali's new criminalisation of same-sex conduct.

The Conversation (15 January 2025), interview with anthropologist Christophe Broqua: Mali’s new penal code — announced October 2024, in force 13 December 2024 — criminalises homosexuality and any citizen seen to encourage it, a sharp escalation under the military junta alongside clampdowns on opposition and media.
US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Mali: official assessment - same-sex conduct not criminalised but significant societal stigma; violence and instability from armed groups.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Mali: documents gender inequality, FGM, corruption, and 'discrimination based on sexual orientation' among other human-rights problems.
